prompt: On the shop's five-point scales, a risk is likely (4) and moderate (3). What is its score?
Why does each step of the likelihood scale carry a description such as "expected about once a year"?

choices.text: To convert the score into money
choices.why: A word scale does not become money; that is the next section.

choices.text: So two people would give the same risk the same score
choices.why: Right. "Likely" has to mean the same thing to finance and to IT.

choices.text: Because auditors require exactly five steps on every scale
choices.why: Five is a common choice, not a requirement.

choices.text: To make the matrix look precise
choices.why: The lesson says it is not precise and need not be.

prompt: A risk scored 5 × 2 and another scored 2 × 5 both total 10. What does the lesson warn the grid hides?
hint: Look at which factor is large.

choices.text: A nuisance is not a catastrophe
choices.why: Right. Same score, different treatment.

choices.text: That the scale should have ten steps
choices.why: More steps would not separate them.

choices.text: That one of the two was scored wrongly
choices.why: Both are legitimate scores.

choices.text: Nothing; equal scores are equal risks
choices.why: That is exactly what the warning is about.

prompt: What is a qualitative matrix good at, according to the lesson?
hint: And what is it bad at?

choices.text: Ranking
choices.why: Right. It answers "what first?".

choices.text: Proving that a risk is gone
choices.why: No matrix proves that.

choices.text: Measuring the exact probability of each event
choices.why: Its scores are judgements, not measurements.

choices.text: Deciding how much to spend on a control
choices.why: That is what it is bad at.

prompt: A laptop worth R$ 7,000 is lost entirely (EF 1), about once every two years. What is the ALE, in reais?
R$ 80,000 is at stake and one attack destroys half of it. What is the SLE, in reais?
A risk has an ALE of R$ 4,000. A control costing R$ 1,500 a year brings the ALE down to R$ 400. By how much, in reais per year, is the shop better off?
hint: The loss removed, minus the cost.

prompt: An ALE of R$ 3,500 a year means what?

choices.text: The shop will lose exactly R$ 3,500 next year
choices.why: Some years lose nothing and some lose more.

choices.text: The cost of the control that would prevent the whole loss
choices.why: The ALE is the loss, before any control.

choices.text: The average yearly loss over many years
choices.why: Right. It is an expectation, not a forecast.

choices.text: The value of the laptop
choices.why: That is the AV.

prompt: The offline backup would cost R$ 5,000 a year instead of R$ 1,500. What does the arithmetic now say?

choices.text: Buy it anyway, because ransomware is severe and the numbers do not capture that
choices.why: Severity is already in the numbers.

choices.text: The ALE rises to R$ 5,000
choices.why: The ALE does not include the control's price.

choices.text: The exposure factor doubles
choices.why: Price does not change how much an attack destroys.

choices.text: The control costs more than the risk it removes
choices.why: Right. Look for a cheaper control or accept.

prompt: What limits the precision of a quantitative assessment?
hint: The lesson puts it in one sentence.

choices.text: The precision of its worst input
choices.why: Right. An ARO of 0.1 is a guess with a range.

choices.text: The number of decimal places in the spreadsheet
choices.why: Decimals do not make a guess more accurate.

choices.text: The size of the organisation
choices.why: A small shop and a bank face the same limit.

choices.text: Whether the currency is reais or dollars
choices.why: Currency is irrelevant.

prompt: Match each action to the treatment it is.

pairs.left: deleting the copies of customers' ID documents and no longer collecting them
signing off the flood risk for a year

prompt: The shop moves card payments to a payment provider. A provider leak exposes the shop's customers. What did the transfer NOT move?
hint: Who do the customers look at?

choices.text: The card numbers
choices.why: Those did move: they never touch the shop's server.

choices.text: The cost of processing payments
choices.why: That is a commercial detail, not the point.

choices.text: The need for any security at the provider
choices.why: The provider carries its share; that is the transfer.

choices.text: Accountability
choices.why: Right. Customers, press and regulator still look at the shop.

prompt: Which treatment is the only one that brings a risk to zero?

choices.text: Avoid
choices.why: Right. No activity, no risk from it.

choices.text: Transfer, through insurance
choices.why: Insurance pays money; the event can still happen.

choices.text: Accept
choices.why: Accepting keeps the risk as it is.

choices.text: Mitigate, with enough controls stacked together
choices.why: Mitigation always leaves residual risk.

prompt: Nobody ever looked at the risk of a burst pipe over the server. It happens. Was the risk accepted?
hint: What three things make an acceptance?

choices.text: Yes, because pipes are a natural threat
choices.why: The source of a threat does not decide acceptance.

choices.text: No; it was ignored, because nothing was written, signed or dated
choices.why: Right. The difference between acceptance and neglect is the paperwork.

choices.text: Yes, since nothing was done about it
choices.why: Doing nothing without deciding is neglect.

choices.text: No, because only IT may accept risks
choices.why: The owner accepts, not IT.

prompt: What is residual risk?

choices.text: A risk transferred to an insurer
choices.why: Transfer is a treatment; residual risk follows any treatment.

choices.text: What remains once the chosen controls are in place
choices.why: Right. And somebody has to accept it.

choices.text: The risk before any control
choices.why: That is inherent risk.

choices.text: Any risk whose score on the matrix has fallen below the appetite of 6
choices.why: That is a comparison with appetite, not a definition.

prompt: After a new password and MFA, R1's residual score is 8. The owners' appetite is 6. What does the lesson say comes next?

choices.text: Nothing; a treatment was applied, so it is done
choices.why: Every treatment ends with accepting what is left, within appetite or by signature.

choices.text: Another control, or the owners sign for 8
choices.why: Right. Taking the portal off the internet brings it to 4.

choices.text: IT accepts the 8, since IT did the work
choices.why: The risk owner decides, not IT.

choices.text: Lower the appetite to 8 for this one risk
choices.why: Raising a threshold for one row is accepting without saying so.

prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: how much risk the organisation will take, set by its leadership
the acceptable deviation for one objective, as a number

right_distractors: the risk transferred to a supplier

prompt: Who owns R1, the risk to the payroll file, and why?

choices.text: ana, because she runs IT and installed the portal
choices.why: IT proposes controls; it does not own the business's risks.

choices.text: bruno, who runs finance
choices.why: Right. The payroll file belongs to finance.

choices.text: Nobody until an incident happens
choices.why: Every risk has an owner from the start.

choices.text: The auditor, who checks the register
choices.why: An auditor reviews; it does not own.

prompt: Why does the register describe a risk with a sentence rather than a word like "portal"?

choices.text: Sentences sort better in a spreadsheet
choices.why: Sorting is not the point.

choices.text: Because a word cannot have an owner
choices.why: Owners are a separate column.

choices.text: So somebody later understands it and checks it is still true
choices.why: Right. The chain from lesson 2 makes it reviewable.

choices.text: Auditors count words
choices.why: They read for meaning.

prompt: A scanner reports 300 findings. How many rows should the register gain?
hint: Findings and risks are different things.

choices.text: 300, one per finding
choices.why: A register of every finding is one nobody reads.

choices.text: Only as many as the findings that create or change a risk
choices.why: Right. Most findings never become a row.

choices.text: One row called "scanner findings"
choices.why: That is a word, not a risk sentence.

choices.text: None, since scanners are not part of risk management
choices.why: Findings feed the register when they create or change a risk.

prompt: Order the steps the lesson follows for one risk.
hint: From writing it down to coming back.
items: write the risk as a sentence
review it on the date set
trap: A treatment chosen before the risk is scored has nothing to be compared with.

prompt: Which of these make an acceptance legitimate? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It has a date to be reviewed
choices.why: One of the three.

choices.text: It is written down
choices.why: One of the three.

choices.text: It is signed by somebody with the authority
choices.why: One of the three.

choices.text: IT agreed to it
choices.why: IT's agreement is not what makes it legitimate.
